title: Signature Packet v3 is not considered secure since 2026-02-01
body:
### What happened?

When installing **kubectl** on Debian 13, according to your [instructions](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/install-kubectl-linux/#kubectl-install-0) you get the following warning message, when launching `apt update` command:

```console
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
Audit: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Sub-process /usr/bin/sqv returned an error code (1), error message is:
   Error: Policy rejected packet type
   Caused by:
       Signature Packet v3 is not considered secure since 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect instead to work without any warning.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Debian 13
- Follow your instruction for installing kubectl on Debian
- Run `apt update`

title: Failed to destroy network for pod from CNI network after reboot
body:
### What happened?

See Also cilium/cilium#40459

When restarting a Node with this example Deamonset (it has to be shareProcessNamespace and privileged)
```
kind: DaemonSet
apiVersion: apps/v1
metadata:
  name: debian
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: debian-slim
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: debian-slim
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: debian
          image:  debian:12-slim
          command: ["/usr/bin/sleep"]
          args: ["infinity"]
          securityContext:
            privileged: true
      shareProcessNamespace: true
```

The Deamonset gets stuck as it is trying to kill the pod before the Reboot
Kubernetes Event:
```
error killing pod: failed to "KillPodSandbox" for "14b3c082-8591-43e5-a9ca-48105a52dfd3" with KillPodSandboxError: "rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to destroy network for pod sandbox k8s_nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-vf6cz_14b3c082-8591-43e5-a9ca-48105a52dfd3_0(a29ea010f0f050d3bfca52098739b734a35a2353621d4bd1e21b427294a3e5e1): error removing pod nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-vf6cz from CNI network \"cilium\": plugin type=\"cilium-cni\" failed (delete): opening netns pinned at : open : no such file or directory: stat netns path \"\": stat : no such file or directory"
```




### What did you expect to happen?

Kill the old Pod and start a new one

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create the Example Deamonset and reboot a node
See that no new pod is started on the Node as it is stuck terminating the previous one

@aojea I'm curious, if the Node is restarted then I would assume that the Pod is no longer present on the Node. For the Pod to be re-established after startup, I'd expect the CNI to receive a CNI ADD. What appears to be happening is instead the Node reboots then there is a CNI DEL. Why does the CNI DEL occur after restart? Is it to provide an opportunity to clean up any state that might persist after reboot?

node reboot, here be dragons , is one of the most complex and unspecified problem as you can see in the number of issues reported,  https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Akubernetes%2Fkubernetes+pods+node+reboot&type=issues 

Beside, this issue requires more information, as it contains additional complexity, the error says

> error killing pod: failed to "KillPodSandbox" for "14b3c082-8591-43e5-a9ca-48105a52dfd3" with KillPodSandboxError: "rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to destroy network for pod sandbox k8s_nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-vf6cz_14b3c082-8591-43e5-a9ca-48105a52dfd3_0(a29ea010f0f050d3bfca52098739b734a35a2353621d4bd1e21b427294a3e5e1): error removing pod nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-vf6cz from CNI network \"cilium\": plugin type=\"cilium-cni\" failed (delete): opening netns pinned at : open : no such file or directory: stat netns path \"\": stat : no such file or directory"

 device plugin has known issues on reboots https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/128043

nvidia device plugin use also to inject oci hooks and other stuff 

so, to really understand what happens if requires to look at the kubelet and crio logs to see what s going on and validate if there is no CNI ADD and why not

My comment about CNI is that is simple but is not associated to the Pod lifecycle, if you see the codebase the CNI DEL is sent in multiple places, if a RunPodSandbox fails, and if you are chained you may get broken, we were hit by this https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/12130 last week .Depending on the pod lifecycle hooks is more reliable, as you not depend on the implementation details of the runtime that differ between crio and containerd, instead you depend on well established parts of the lifecycle.

@hoferbeck I can take a look to the kubelet and crio logs if you can upload it, if @joestringer is right and there is no CNI ADD is somethinn we need to investigate

title: Clock synchronization causes the token to be not valid yet
body:
### What happened?

We have some clusters in isolated environments that, after running for a long time, need to synchronize with an external clock. During this process, a time jump may occur, and if the time is adjusted forward, it can result in tokens not yet being valid.
```go
// requiresRefresh returns true if the token is older than 80% of its total
// ttl, or if the token is older than 24 hours.
func (m *Manager) requiresRefresh(tr *authenticationv1.TokenRequest) bool {
        if tr.Spec.ExpirationSeconds == nil {
                cpy := tr.DeepCopy()
                cpy.Status.Token = ""
                klog.ErrorS(nil, "Expiration seconds was nil for token request", "tokenRequest", cpy)
                return false
        }
        now := m.clock.Now()
        exp := tr.Status.ExpirationTimestamp.Time
        iat := exp.Add(-1 * time.Duration(*tr.Spec.ExpirationSeconds) * time.Second)

        jitter := time.Duration(rand.Float64()*maxJitter.Seconds()) * time.Second
        if now.After(iat.Add(maxTTL - jitter)) {
                return true
        }
        // Require a refresh if within 20% of the TTL plus a jitter from the expiration time.
        if now.After(exp.Add(-1*time.Duration((*tr.Spec.ExpirationSeconds*20)/100)*time.Second - jitter)) {
                return true
        }
        return false
}
``` 
After reviewing the code（k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/token/token_manager.go）, I found that when checking whether a token needs to be updated, it only considers whether it has expired and whether it meets the rotation requirements. It does not check if the current time is earlier than the token's issued time, which confuses me.

### What did you expect to happen?

iI believe that the scenario where the current time is earlier than the issued time should also be checked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Adjust the cluster clock forward by 1 hour.

title: Deprecated AppArmor annotation field not yet removed
body: ### What happened? Starting on Kubernetes v1.30, the location where to specify [AppArmor profiles](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/apparmor/) changed. Prior to v1.30, it used to be located in an annotation, but after the upgrade, AppArmor profiles are now specified within the `securityContext` fields of the manifest, as the annotation field for AppArmor [is now deprecated](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/apparmor/#securing-a-pod). As part of another thing I'm working on, I went to check the [PSS baseline policy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/#baseline) docs as it collects the syntax of all the places where the AppArmor may appear within a given manifest. It currently points out that the AppArmor profile in the annotation is still a restricted field: This felt odd, as the annotation is deprecated, but when I went to check this on a Kubernetes 1.33 cluster, the annotation is still restricted by the PSS baseline with an error similar to the below: ``` Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "test-apparmor-pod.yaml": pods "apparmor-unconfined-pod" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "baseline:v1.33": forbidden AppArmor profiles (container "nginx" and annotation must not set AppArmor profile type to "Unconfined", "container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx="unconfined"") ``` The next step was to review the [Kubernetes deprecation policy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/). The second bullet point of `Rule #4a: API lifetime is determined by the API stability level` reads as follows: > Beta API versions are deprecated no more than 9 months or 3 minor releases after introduction (whichever is longer), and are no longer served 9 months or 3 minor releases after deprecation (whichever is longer) And I understand that the annotation is within the scope of the deprecation policy as per the [initial section of the same document](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/#deprecating-parts-of-the-api), which reads like the following: > The following rules govern the deprecation of elements of the API. This includes: > - REST resources (aka API objects) > - Fields of REST resources > - Annotations on REST resources, including "beta" annotations but not including "alpha" annotations. > [...] Given that the deprecation was introduced in v1.30, I understand it should have been removed in v1.33. I looked for issues within this repository and the website one but could not find references to this topic. The fact that the annotation field is still being checked introduces a level of confusion and a potential sense of false security. ### What did you expect to happen? The deprecated AppArmor annotation should be removed, as per the deprecation policy. Consequently, adding the AppArmor profile setting to the manifest on the annotation field should be ignored altogether since that functionality will not be there once the removal has finished. The accompanying documentation in the PSS page should also be updated to reflect this. In the meantime, if there's is some sort of tracking page it would also be helpful that it was added to the documentation, as to avoid more people getting confused by this. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Use `kind` to deploy a local cluster on v1.33: ``` cat > kind-config.yaml < test-apparmor-pod.yaml < ```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.33.2 Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 Server Version: v1.33.1 ``` ### Cloud provider N/A ### OS version _No response_ ### Install tools _No response_ ### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable) ### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

title: conversion-gen generates code that leads to panics when fields are accessed after conversion
body:
### What happened?

As the title says, conversion-gen has a bug that generates incorrect conversion code.

struct in the old apiVersion:
```go
type JSONSchemaProps struct {
	Items      *JSONSchemaProps           `json:"items,omitempty"`
	Properties map[string]JSONSchemaProps `json:"properties,omitempty"`
	AllOf      []JSONSchemaProps          `json:"allOf,omitempty"`

	ExclusiveMaximum bool `json:"exclusiveMaximum,omitempty"`
}
```

struct in the new apiVersion: (`ExclusiveMaximum` was changed from `bool` to `*bool`)
```go
type JSONSchemaProps struct {
	Items      *JSONSchemaProps           `json:"items,omitempty"`
	Properties map[string]JSONSchemaProps `json:"properties,omitempty"`
	AllOf      []JSONSchemaProps          `json:"allOf,omitempty"`

	ExclusiveMaximum *bool `json:"exclusiveMaximum,omitempty"`
}
```

Generated conversion code:
```go
func autoConvert_v1beta2_JSONSchemaProps_To_v1beta1_JSONSchemaProps(in *v1beta2.JSONSchemaProps, out *JSONSchemaProps, s conversion.Scope) error {
	out.Items = (*JSONSchemaProps)(unsafe.Pointer(in.Items))
	out.Properties = *(*map[string]JSONSchemaProps)(unsafe.Pointer(&in.Properties))
	out.AllOf = *(*[]JSONSchemaProps)(unsafe.Pointer(&in.AllOf))
	if err := v1.Convert_Pointer_bool_To_bool(&in.ExclusiveMaximum, &out.ExclusiveMaximum, s); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return nil
}
```

Issue: 
`out.Items = (*JSONSchemaProps)(unsafe.Pointer(in.Items))` is wrong (similar for `Properties` and `AllOf`).
`autoConvert_v1beta2_JSONSchemaProps_To_v1beta1_JSONSchemaProps` should be called instead.

Accessing the `ExlusiveMaximum` field after conversion leads to a panic.

Full example can be seen here: https://github.com/sbueringer/conversion-gen-panic-repro (just checkout and run `make test`).


### What did you expect to happen?

conversion-gen should generate correct code

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Full example can be seen here: https://github.com/sbueringer/conversion-gen-panic-repro (just checkout and run `make test`).


### Kubernetes version

conversion-gen v0.33.0

Related Slack thread: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1752170662367799 (but all relevant information is contained in this issue)

E2-micro is a shared-core VM with 12.5% of CPU time, likely contributed to the CPU starvation and timeout in this case.

This might also be related to the containerd 2.0 image load performance degradation: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/11726

Currently there is a 30s timeout on image loading. From experiment changing this value to 300s fixed the issue, and e2-micro nodes can be bootstrapped successfully.

<details>

```
# $1: Full path of the docker image
function try-load-docker-image {
  local -r img=$1
  echo "Try to load docker image file ${img}"
  # Temporarily turn off errexit, because we don't want to exit on first failure.
  set +e
  local -r max_attempts=5
  local -i attempt_num=1

  if [[ "${CONTAINER_RUNTIME_NAME:-}" == "containerd" || "${CONTAINERD_TEST:-}"  == "containerd" ]]; then
    load_image_command=${LOAD_IMAGE_COMMAND:-ctr -n=k8s.io images import}
  else
    load_image_command="${LOAD_IMAGE_COMMAND:-}"
  fi

  # Deliberately word split load_image_command
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  #### Change this to 300s
  until timeout 30 ${load_image_command} "${img}"; do
    if [[ "${attempt_num}" == "${max_attempts}" ]]; then
      echo "Fail to load docker image file ${img} using ${load_image_command} after ${max_attempts} retries. Exit!!"
      exit 1
    else
      attempt_num=$((attempt_num+1))
      sleep 5
    fi
  done
  # Re-enable errexit.
  set -e
}
```

</details>

The node should be bootstrapped successfully.

nodes.title: Make kubelet token cache UID-aware to prevent stale tokens after service account recreation
nodes.body:
Fixes an issue where the kubelet token cache could return stale tokens when a service account is deleted and recreated with the same name. The cache was keyed only by namespace and service account name, causing it to return expired tokens for the new service account.

fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132802

```release-note
Fix kubelet token cache returning stale tokens when service accounts are recreated with the same name. The token cache is now UID-aware and the new `TokenRequestServiceAccountUIDValidation` feature gate (Beta, enabled by default) validates the TokenRequest UID when set matches the service account UID.
```

title: kube-proxy incorrectly logs "Ignoring same-zone topology hints" when there are no endpoints
body:
### What happened?

We recently upgraded our EKS cluster from 1.32 to 1.33, and noticed an unusually high volume of logs coming from kube-proxy like this:
```
Ignoring same-zone topology hints for service since no hints were provided for zone
```

We have not enabled zone-aware routing or hints (either by .spec.trafficDistribution or by the older annotation) for any service and were surprised to see this log message. The service has no endpoints in the endpoint slice.

<details>
<summary> Example service YAML</summary>

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.10.129.215
  clusterIPs:
  - 10.10.129.215
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  ipFamilies:
  - IPv4
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    app: my-service
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

</details>

<details>
<summary> Example endpointslice YAML</summary>

```yaml
addressType: IPv4
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
endpoints: null
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  annotations:
    endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time: "2024-10-29T09:45:37Z"
  creationTimestamp: "2024-10-11T12:46:31Z"
  generateName: my-service-
  generation: 397
  labels:
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io
  name: my-service-qwq6l
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: true
    controller: true
    kind: Service
    name: my-service
    uid: 2c3edd43-8041-4aa6-ac2b-8e5508d7c6ff
  resourceVersion: "5958818965"
  uid: b485a7f7-6363-4b5f-b3f2-d6eb394ac034
ports: null
```

</details>

Looking through [topology.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/topology.go#L195), it looks like we intend to log this line when all endpoints in the endpoint slice have zone hints, and the zone parameter is not empty. However, since we initialise allEndpointsHaveZoneHints to true then loop through the endpoints to set it to false, we will inadvertently log this line for any endpoint slices that are empty.

I think the simple fix is to exit `topologyModeFromHints` early and return an empty string if no endpoints are found. I am happy to contribute this patch

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect to not see this log line for empty endpoint slices

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I have not tried it, but I presume you could create a service with no endpoints and see that kube-proxy logs this log line

nodes.title: Fix volume limit e2e test cleanup
nodes.body:
Pass the local test state to `cleanupTest()` as a pointer. It is mostly empty at the point of calling  `DeferCleanup(cleanupTest, ...)`, so using `ginkgo.DeferCleanup(cleanupTest, ..., l.podNames, ...)` just passes empty `podNames` to the cleanup and the test pods are not deleted.
`l.podNames` gets populated later and the cleanup must use the updated one.

And now that the cleanup actually does something, fix the error handling in it.

title: [PodLevelResources] Update Downward API defaulting logic for `resource.limits`
body:
Using the Downward API's [resourceFieldRef](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/downward-api/#downwardapi-resourcefieldref), you can inject values specified in `resources.limits`, such as CPU, memory, or ephemeral storage into environment variables.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: downward-api-resource-limits
spec:
  containers:
  - name: sleep
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo CPU_LIMIT=$CPU_LIMIT; echo MEMORY_LIMIT=$MEMORY_LIMIT; sleep infinity"]
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 128Mi
    env:
    - name: CPU_LIMIT
      valueFrom:
        resourceFieldRef:
          resource: limits.cpu
    - name: MEMORY_LIMIT
      valueFrom:
        resourceFieldRef:
          resource: limits.memory
```

Currently, when container-level resource limits were not specified and the Downward API was used to set environment variables referencing them, the node's allocatable resources were used in the defaulting logic.
With the introduction of the Pod Level Resources feature, this behavior should be updated as outlined in the comment.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b2f27c0649fc0f3d2a4a6dd29135ecc81781f7e4/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_resources.go#L33-L34

title: [PodLevelResources] Validation for Windows OS
body:
PodLevelResources feature is not supported on Windows OS. Add the necessary validation logic to reject pods for Windows.

From the KEP #2837, until full Windows support for pod-level resource specifications is implemented, the behavior for pods, with pod-level resources, targeting Windows is as follows:

- API Server Validation: If the spec.os.name field in the Pod specification is explicitly set to "windows", the Kubernetes API server will generally reject the pod during validation.

    Add the following logic in [validatePodResources](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c14c5722a2e8f357dac32be1e1018925b05158e0/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L4302)
       // windows pods are not supported.
	if oldPod.Spec.OS != nil && oldPod.Spec.OS.Name == core.Windows && pod level resources are set {
		return field.ErrorList....
	}

- Kubelet Admission: The Kubelet running on a Windows node would reject the pod, with pod-level resources, during admission.
     
     Add IsPodLevelResourcesAllowed in features_windows.go, features_linux.go and features_unsupported.go (example - [ref](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Akubernetes%2Fkubernetes+%22func+IsInPlacePodVerticalScalingAllowed%22&type=code)  
    and call this method from [SyncPod](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1680008ddc74dc7141a4c26fa17b99d5dde99d4d/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1134)) if pod level resources are set in the spec

title: [Pod Level Resources] Pod-level resource validation fails when container-level is set for other resource
body:
### What happened?

When a Kubernetes Pod defines resources.requests at the Pod level, but only specifies a subset of the supported resources requested by its containers (e.g., only cpu at the Pod level, while a container requests memory), Kubernetes' validation implicitly assigns a request of "0" for the unstated resource (e.g., memory) at the Pod level. This "0" value then triggers a validation error because it's less than the actual aggregated request from the containers, even though the user might expect the Pod to implicitly aggregate the container's memory request.

```
 "pod" is invalid: spec.resources.requests[memory]: Invalid value: "0": must be greater than or equal to aggregate container requests of 10Mi
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When a user defines resource requests at the container level, Kubernetes already aggregates these requests internally to determine the total resource needs of the Pod. If the Pod.spec.resources.requests field is present, but only specifies a subset of resources (e.g., cpu but not memory), the intuitive expectation is that Kubernetes would implicitly aggregate the memory request from the containers, rather than defaulting the Pod's memory request to 0.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ccf291b50166ce82204486aae6a626a30b469182/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L4406 needs to be fixed to compare container aggregates with pod-level values only if pod-level value for that resource is set.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Enable PodLevelResources feature gate on apiserver, scheduler and kubelet, and create the following pod
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-bug
spec:
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "300m"  # Pod-level CPU request
  containers:
  - name: sleep-infinity
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-memory: 10Mi 
```

title: `kube_codegen.sh` does not resolve "local" GOBIN when invoking the tools
body:
### What happened?

Required binaries are installed using `go install`, which relies on the predefined `GOBIN`. But when codegen tools are invoked in the script, the resolved `gobin` variable might not be pointing to the right location, as it's only resolving the environment variable (`$GOBIN`) or fall back to `$GOPATH/bin` explicitly, missing the value which might be set for `go env GOBIN` without exporting it.

The correct location is used, and so the binary is invoked (or the desired version of it).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Using `go env GOBIN` to locate where codegen binaries should be installed provides a more reliable and flexible solution.

- Picks up a user's custom `GOBIN` whether it's set as an environment variable or only in `go env`
- Falls back to `$GOPATH/bin` if no `GOBIN` is defined

This handles setups (e.g. using tools like [`mise`](https://mise.jdx.dev/lang/go.html)) where `GOBIN` is configured internally but not exported.

The old lookup missed those internally configured values and could fail if the binary isn't present in the assumed location (or worse invoke the wrong codegen binary :)).

title: DRA resource claim controller: fails to clean up deleted ResourceClaims on startup
body:
### What happened?

* kube-controller-manager is stopped.
* A allocated claim with one pod in ReservedFor is marked as deleted (but not removed yet because of the finalizer).
* That pod gets deleted, terminates and gets removed.
* kube-controller-manager is restarted.

The ResourceClaim controllers logs:
```
I0616 15:55:01.290991       1 controller.go:390] "not enqueing deleted claim" logger="resourceclaim-controller" claim="dra-6273/external-claim-2"
I0616 15:55:01.291019       1 controller.go:401] "unrelated to any known pod" logger="resourceclaim-controller" claim="dra-6273/external-claim-2"
```

It does not do anything, so the claim remains pending.

This was triggered while working on upgrade/downgrade scenarios.

/wg device-management
/sig node

### What did you expect to happen?

The ResourceClaim controller should remove the pod from ReservedFor, the allocation, and the finalizer, thus unblocking the removal of the ResourceClaim.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not easy, needs WIP test.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a regression introduced by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127661.

The logic here is inverted:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/c2524cbf9b49f034053f758401ec3b08a4504e0e/pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go#L330

The correct expression is `deleted := newObj == nil`.


This causes the enqueuing of the claim for processing to get skipped in

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c2524cbf9b49f034053f758401ec3b08a4504e0e/pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go#L372-L377

Normally, this gets mitigated by pod removal which also has the desired effect, but in this particular case that removal is never observed - the pod is already gone when the kube-controller-manager starts.

What happens is that the IPAddress is created but later in the process the Service creation fails, but the IP cleanup races with the repairip loop `repairip.go` and emits the event, then the `ipallocator.go` fails to delete the address because is already removed.

```
I0624 21:38:14.671700       1 ipallocator.go:374] error releasing ip 10.96.104.42 : ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io "10.96.104.42" not found
```

so the IP allocated is WAI, it worked that way before, it seems the only problem is that is emitting an event, or are there any other issues @liubog2008 ?

> so the IP allocated is WAI, it worked that way before, it seems the only problem is that is emitting an event, or are there any other issues [@liubog2008](https://github.com/liubog2008) ?

@aojea In my case, there are no other issues. (Event emitting is the only problem)

Below are the details in my case:
- I am implementing operator, which has a `Service` creation logic.
- It does not check existance of the target `Service` when creating it, and just ignores "Already Exists" error.
- As operator periodically executes the reconcile loop, error `Event` emitting happens repeatedly.

> @liubog2008 why do you want to configure/create default/kubernetes service?

@aroradaman Just an example for easily reproducing.
@aojea I think the problem is when I try to create an existing service, apiserver should reject the request and not create anything.
My use case is same as @hoony9x

> [@aojea](https://github.com/aojea) I think the problem is when I try to create an existing service, apiserver should reject the request and not create anything.

Service is the only API that implement a transaction and uses the IPAddress object to guarantee consistency across the cluster,  you can read more in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/1880-multiple-service-cidrs/README.md

The allocation of the IP happens first, and if the service creation fails, the IP is deleted, is an internal operation, if you see the log when the Service fails to be created the transaction is reverted ...  the repair loop is faster and emits an event. In this case the problem is that the Service already exist, so the repair loop does not wait for the transaction to finish and removes the IP because checks that the ClusterIP of the Service does not match the object, hence it is a leak

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec80dcaf3892d0cf89e4fd7b1ea60300fb417d8a/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/controller/repairip.go#L492-L529

The problem is that we should not try to allocate an IP address for a Service that already exists and has IPs allocated, and fail at that moment ... but Service pipeline is complex and allocation happens at `BeginCreate`, @thockin @liggitt do you know if we can detect that at this stage?

> in version 1.33+, the resource `ip` created and then deleted.

that is not a problem, those resources are owned by the apiserver so it is ok

> can this be solved by adding a judgment in BeginCreate

does not looks like a great pattern to implement, and can be also racy, in multiple master environment, services can be created/deleted/updated in parallel

> does not looks like a great pattern to implement, and can be also racy, in multiple master environment, services can be created/deleted/updated in parallel

I think it's enough? It can fix most unnecessary ip allocation by a lower cost (create a new ip vs get a svc from cache). And just keep the `repairip` to avoid race.

> The problem is that we should not try to allocate an IP address for a Service that already exists and has IPs allocated, and fail at that moment ... but Service pipeline is complex and allocation happens at `BeginCreate`, [@thockin](https://github.com/thockin) [@liggitt](https://github.com/liggitt) do you know if we can detect that at this stage?

No, trying to detect existence before persisting to etcd ~doubles the cost of creates and makes a new race that can still happen if two creates are attempted simultaneously.

I think it's better to tweak the repair loop to avoid spurious warnings in this scenario... perhaps by doing something like:
* If an IPAddress is observed with a creation timestamp *after* the service it references, delay repair loop processing of the IPAddress for a few seconds (1? 5?) in case the IPAddress was provisioned and then immediately cleaned up as part of a transaction.
Hi, I have tried the fix @liggitt proposed and it is removing the errors. @aroradaman I am happy to open a PR if you haven't already started working on the fix.

nodes.title: service-ip-alloc: delay ip processing on service recreate
nodes.body:
Service storage implements transactions. It creates an IPAddress object first and then creates the Service object, and if the Service object already exists the complete transaction is reverted. There can be race conditions when the repair loop picks up the new IPAddress object for reconciliation before the transaction is reverted. This leads to spurious IPAddressWrongReference warnings, to suppress these warnings we delay the processing of the new IPAddress object by 5 seconds. The service allocation creates the IPAddress object before creating the Service object, we easily identify this scenario when Service object is created before the IPAddress object.

I think this may be because of SuccessPolicy feature.

Seeing (2s) here:
```
NAME                         STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
suspended-zero-completions   Running   0/0                      2s
```
I assume the job is still "Running", because some pods are still terminating.

Since 1.31 Kubernetes adds conditions which indicate the fate of the Job (SuccessCriteriaMet or FailureTarget), but awaits with adding the terminal conditions (Complete, Failed) until all Pods are fully terminated.

This was stated in the release note for [1.31](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.31.md):
```
Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet
```
If you can confirm the Job eventually obtains the terminal condition, then this is WAI.
/sig apps

I tested the same job and the behavior between v1.31 and v1.32 is different when `spec.completions` is 0 and `spec.suspend` is true.

This is the output for v1.31:

```bash
NAME                         STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
suspended-zero-completions   Complete   0/0           0s         3m31s
```

There are no pods created as expected, and the job status is updated to `Complete` right away.

For v1.32, it stays in a running state with no pods created.

```bash
NAME                         STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
suspended-zero-completions   Running   0/0                      10m
```

I looked at the controller logs, and for v1.32, we have this error:

```
E0610 00:44:48.650216       1 job_controller.go:631] "Unhandled Error" err="syncing job: tracking status: removing uncounted pods from status: Job.batch \"suspended-zero-completions\" is invalid: status.startTime: Required value: startTime is required for finished job" logger="UnhandledError"
```

Which means that the job is completed (as the completion count is zero out of zero), but the start time is not set (as the job is suspended). It seems that because of this error, the status of the job cannot be updated to `Complete`.

My question is why do we allow the creation of jobs with `completions=0`? In the documentation we clearly indicate that this value is a non-zero positive.

> My question is why do we allow the creation of jobs with completions=0?

That's a good question. A job with `completions=0` would not run any Pods in any case. @jb-metzger do you have any use-case for this setup?

The options I see:
1. strengthen Job validation to prevent setting `completions=0`
2. relax Job validation to do not reject setting "Complete" condition when there is no `status.startTime` when completions=0 and suspend=true
3.  update Job controller to ensure it sets startTime whenever it wants to set the Complete condition, probably around [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1509) 

I would be leaning to (3.) because. Strengthening validation (1.) is always hard, you never know what use cases people have. For example one that comes to my mind is just to trigger JobTemplate validation and defaulting without creating Pods (so that later the JobTemplate can be safely used with completions > 0). (2.) seems more work than (3.) .

Well, it is a bit, but so is setting  "CompletionTime" without "StartTime", imo. 

Looking at the validation rules (2.) will be more difficult, and thus risky fix, than to implement (3.).

I have some spare cycles to assist.

After discussing with @mimowo, I could submit an integration test which reproduces it, and take it from there depending on the approach which will be agreed.

> As I checked the documentation and API comments, I could not find the non-zero specifications to Job, while Parallel Job has non-zero completions specifications

Yeah I think what I saw before was only for Parallel jobs. Still, I think it could have been added to the doc.

> The options I see:
> 
> 1. strengthen Job validation to prevent setting `completions=0`
> 2. relax Job validation to do not reject setting "Complete" condition when there is no `status.startTime` when completions=0 and suspend=true
> 3. update Job controller to ensure it sets startTime whenever it wants to set the Complete condition, probably around [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1509)
> 
> I would be leaning to (3.) because. Strengthening validation (1.) is always hard, you never know what use cases people have. For example one that comes to my mind is just to trigger JobTemplate validation and defaulting without creating Pods (so that later the JobTemplate can be safely used with completions > 0). (2.) seems more work than (3.) .

(3.) makes sense but it is a bit strange to set the startTime and completeTime together :?

Another option that makes more sense to me is to set the startTime when we do it normally:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1a200abf92ac69abc468c48fb727f76ab9568d6a/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L913-L916

It can be something like this:

```go
if job.Status.StartTime == nil {
	if !jobSuspended(&job) || (job.Spec.Completions != nil && *job.Spec.Completions == 0) {
		now := metav1.NewTime(jm.clock.Now())
		job.Status.StartTime = &now
	}
}
```

Meaning that the startTime of the job should be set if the job is not suspended or it is already completed.
I have opened the fix PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132614. PTAL

It looks like Michal is working on this issue.

/assign @mimowo

@jb-metzger would you be able to test / confirm the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132614) fixes the issue e2e? It could help us to support backporting, see [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132614#issuecomment-3025038826).

I've opened the cherry-picks:
- [1.33](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132728)
- [1.32](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132727)

I have tested the fix myself on a kind cluster using the Job spec from the issue description, the status is as expected:

```yaml
  status:
    completionTime: "2025-07-04T15:38:17Z"
    conditions:
    - lastProbeTime: "2025-07-04T15:38:17Z"
      lastTransitionTime: "2025-07-04T15:38:17Z"
      message: Reached expected number of succeeded pods
      reason: CompletionsReached
      status: "True"
      type: SuccessCriteriaMet
    - lastProbeTime: "2025-07-04T15:38:17Z"
      lastTransitionTime: "2025-07-04T15:38:17Z"
      message: Reached expected number of succeeded pods
      reason: CompletionsReached
      status: "True"
      type: Complete
    ready: 0
    terminating: 0
    uncountedTerminatedPods: {}
```
I also tested the analogous Job by "Indexed" and it passed too.

/kind regression
since it started in 1.32
@mimowo Do you still need my confirmation? If yes, how can I best test it? Do I have to build kubernetes myself here or is the version in a public registry?

@jb-metzger thanks for reaching out. Actually, the fix is already applied and cherry-picked and released, but your test will be great. 

The fix is part of master, but also, as the "Fix validation for Job with suspend=true, and completions=0 to set the Complete condition. (#132727, @mimowo) [SIG Apps and Testing]" entry:
- [1.33.3](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.33.md)
- [1.32.7](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.32.md)

The changelog contains links to the images you could use for testing, for example for [1.32](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.32.md#container-images).
@mimowo I can confirm that 1.33.3 and 1.32.7 resolve the regression.

title: Service Conflict When Using ClusterIP Port 31000 and NodePort Services Using Same Port
body:
### What happened?

We’re experiencing an intermittent issue when running a Kubernetes service configured with ClusterIP and specifying port 31000. Occasionally, the service becomes inaccessible or fails to function properly.
Upon investigation, we’ve observed this typically happens when another user in the cluster creates a NodePort service that also uses port 31000. It seems there's a conflict at the node level, even though our service is of type ClusterIP.


### What did you expect to happen?

* Kubernetes version: v1.27.16
* Service type: ClusterIP with port 31000
* Observed behavior: Our service randomly fails or becomes inaccessible when others create NodePort services using the same port.
* Expected behavior: ClusterIP services should not conflict with NodePort services even if using the same port, unless explicitly configured to share.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  labels:
    app: nginx-nodeport
  name: nginx-nodeport
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 31000
    targetPort: 31000
    protocol: TCP
    nodePort: 31000
  selector:
    app: nginx-nodeport
  type: NodePort 
```

### Anything else we need to know?

you are using ipvs, IIRC this is a known issue with ipvs but somebody more knowledgeable should confirm

/area ipvs
/sig network

> We’re experiencing an intermittent issue when running a Kubernetes service configured with ClusterIP and specifying port 31000

Did you notice that it only occurred when both TCP connections used the same source port? 

your_service:50000 -> clusterip:30001
your_service:50000 -> nodePort:30001

We have tried to reproduce the issue where service of type ClusterIP exists with port 31000. When we attempted to create a service of type NodePort with nodePort as 31000, ClusterIP service broke.

By nodeport service we mean the dummy service with backend pods and that service is not used by anyone it just for our troubleshooting purposes.

`  ports:
    name: blobstore
    port: 31000
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 31000
  selector:
    release: ds-blobstore-XXXX-AAAA-XXX
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  labels:
    app: nginx-nodeport
  name: nginx-nodeport
spec:
  ports:
    - nodePort: 31000
      port: 31000
      protocol: TCP
      targetPort: 31000
  type: NodePort `

As @aojea said, there are some known problems like this with ipvs.

The ipvs kube-proxy mode is now sort of deprecated (probably to become officially deprecated soon), and we recommend that people who are currently using it should [try the new nftables mode instead](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/02/28/nftables-kube-proxy/) (though that may not help you, since it looks like you're using 1.27, which is before the nftables mode was added).

The iptables mode is definitely less buggy than ipvs, and is much more performant than it was a few years ago, so if your cluster isn't too huge, you could also try just switching from ipvs to iptables.

Actually... another possibility is to set the [`nodePortAddresses`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#service-nodeport-custom-listen-address) in your kube-proxy config. That should prevent it from trying to accept NodePort connections on cluster IPs.

/close

title: kubelet podresources API incorrectly reports memory assignments of terminated pods
body:
### What happened?

The kubelet podresources endpoint returns allocated exclusive resources to active pods. The endpoint incorrectly returns resources allocated to terminated pods.

If it’s using `GetAllocatableResources`, it seems like information about `Completed` pods might also be included. Since `List` is supposed to return information only for running pods, including `Completed` pods would seem like a bug.
@toVersus It uses List() function

/triage accepted

the problem here is how the podresources API implementation fetches data from the resource managers. Looking at the implementation here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/podresources/server_v1.go#L60 we take care of syncing the device allocation data before querying the resource managers to return their pod->devices assignment. This is needed because otherwise the resource managers would do the cleanup asynchronously, so the `List` call will return incorrect data.

But we don't do this syncing neither for CPUs or for memory, so when we report these we will get stale data as this issue demonstrates.

For CPU manager, we however have the reconcile loop which cleans the stale data periodically. Turns out this timing interplay was actually the reason the existing issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423 seemed fixed (see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423#issuecomment-2786891218). But it's actually timing. If in the reproducer we set the `cpuManagerReconcilePeriod` to a time very high (>= 5 minutes), then the issue still reproduces against current master branch (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/podresources_test.go#L983).

We can fix in two ways: adding explicit syncs for cpu and memory like we do for devices.
Or, fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423 making the `List` endpoint iterate over the active pods (vs all of them). This is the best fix because it makes the endpoint consistent with what the resource managers are doing.
`List` is using all the pods known about: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3135 -> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/pod/pod_manager.go#L215
But all the resource managers are using the list of active pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1666 -> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L198

Now: I read the warning in the docstring of GetActivePods and still having the endpoint using a different podset wrt the resource managers with the related desync causes way more harm than good. I can't really see a good reason to. And still, we can and probably should have a way to preserve the old behavior to zero the chance to break users of the API depending on the old behavior

/priority important-longterm

So, we have the following options to fix:

1.    fix the issues with this approach implemented in #132028 
2.    fix the issue with a different approach: sync the state before each List call, like we do for devices. Still pretty much contained, adds lock contention
3.    option 1, add a feature gate, without a KEP (benefits unclear: all changes here are opt-in anyway)
4.    option 2, add a feature gate, without a KEP
5.    file a new KEP. If we file a new KEP I'd rather propose a new endpoint (ListActive? ListAllocatedResources?) fixing all the known issues of the List endpoint. I really do think this KEP should start beta, as there are no unknowns (and no risks, btw, being a new additive and partially overlapping endpoint)

nodes.title: podresources: list: use active pods
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The podresources API List implementation uses the internal data of the  resource managers as source of truth. But it iterates over the full list of pods known by the kubelet. Differently, all the resource managers do their internal sync using the list of active pods, fetched each reconciliation step using a helper function.
This causes the `List` endpoint to return incorrect data, because it has a view of the world different from what the resource managers actually have.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #132020
Fixes #119423
Fixes #131999

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
We need to acknowledge the the [warning in the docstring of GetActivePods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L194). Arguably, having the endpoint using a different podset than the resource manager causes way more harm than good because of the desync.
And arguably, it's better to fix this issue in just one place instead of having the `List` use a different pod set for unclear reason. For these reasons, while important, I don't think the warning per se invalidated this change.

We need to further acknowledge the `List` endpoint used the full pod list since its inception. So, we will add a way in the `v1` endpoint to preserve the old behavior to zero the chance to break users of the API depending on the old behavior. 

The old `v1alpha1` endpoint will be not modified intentionally.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Change the node-local podresources API endpoint to only consider of active pods. Because this fix changes a long-established behavior, users observing a regressions can use the KubeletPodResourcesListUseActivePods feature gate (default on) to restore the old behavior. Please file an issue if you encounter problems and have to use the Feature Gate.
```

title: kube-proxy: externalTrafficPolicy:Local and proxy-mode=nftables blackholes pods traffic to external IPs
body:
### What happened?

When using kube-proxy on nftables mode and specify a `LoadBalancer` Service with `externalTrafficPolicy:Local` that has an ExternalIP assigned, kube-proxy will create an entry in the kube-proxy ip nftable that will drop traffic to that external IP, like:

```
        map no-endpoint-services {
                type ipv4_addr . inet_proto . inet_service : verdict
                comment "vmap to drop or reject packets to services with no endpoints"
                elements = { 
                             10.88.1.2 . tcp . 80 comment "sys-ingress-priv/internal-ingress-controller-v2:web" : drop,
```

As a result, any pod on the host cannot send traffic to the external IP of the LoadBalancer.

### What did you expect to happen?

On nodes where no workload is present, traffic should not be dropped but load balanced by kube proxy to the target Service endpoints.
This will also bring consistency with how other modes work, as this issue was addressed both for ipvs (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93456)
and iptables (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/77523) modes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run kube-proxy on nftables mode and try hitting a `LoadBalancer` Service `ExternalIP` from within a pod running in a node that does not have ready endpoints of the target service

### Anything else we need to know?

@kubernetes/sig-network-bugs
Simmilar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/75262 but for `nftables` mode

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR fixes priorities of nftables filter chains which kube-proxy installs. We currently have 5 filter chains
1. filter-prerouting (-110)
2. filter-forward (-110)
3. filter-input (-110)
4. filter-output (-110)
5. filter-output-post-dnat (-90)

The first 4 chains operates at a priority lower than DNAT to allow filtering on pre-dnated destination IP and port. This filtering is only used in `filter-prerouting` and `filter-output` chain. But with this the locally originated traffic which should not be subjected external traffic policies is subjected to external traffic policies. 

With this PR we are adding a new chain ` filter-output-pre-dnat` that will operate on pre-dnat priority, and we are merging `filter-output-post-dnat ` into `filter-output`. We are also setting priorities of ` filter-forward`, ` filter-input` and `filter-output` to 0 to short circuit local traffic to external addresses of the service.

1. filter-prerouting-pre-dnat (-110)
2. filter-output-pre-dnat (-110)
3. filter-forward (0)
4. filter-input (0)
5. filter-output (0)

body:
### What happened?

I'm using AWS EKS 1.31. I was doing some tests with `topologySpreadConstraints` and I've noticed that the API Server behaves differently on `Deployments` and `StatefulSets` objects.

title: Does the cpu static policy option of PreferAlignByUncoreCache only support even CPU counts?
body:
### What happened?

When I assign an odd number of CPUs and less than a full uncorecache, this policy cannot assign the cpu properly. I do not know if this option only support even number CPU by design or it is a bug.

For example, 1core:2cpus, cache0: 0-8 cpus. If I assign 7cpus in the pod spec, `takePartialUncore` cannot take any cpus.

The below method only assign even number CPU during SMT enabled scenario.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2ac0bdf360cf2529a3675c7012d0bf415e1051f3/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_assignment.go#L558-L579

assign 7cpus in cache0.

nodes.body:
/sig node
cc @swatisehgal @ffromani

> cache0: 0-8 cpus, SMT enabled. And then using takePartialUncore to acquire 7 cpus, it will fail.

Can you provide more details of the failure? Is the failure SMTAlignment error?

Do you have both `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` and `full-pcpus-only` policy options enabled? 

With `full-pcpu-only` policy option we restrict the CPU Manager core allocation algorithm to full physical cores only. In case you have it enabled and are requesting number of CPUs (7 in your case) that is not multiple of cpusPerCore (2) then the failure is expected.

> Can you provide more details of the failure? Is the failure SMTAlignment error?
> 
It's not a SMTAlignment error, and kubelet will not report an error. Because although this method does not allocate an odd number of CPUs, there is a fallback strategy that will allocate the remaining available CPUs. While no error occurs, the CPUs actually allocated are not aligned by uncore cache, meaning the `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` option is not effectively applied.

```go
// for example: cpu request/limit: 7
// 3 := 7/2
numCoresNeeded := a.numCPUsNeeded / a.topo.CPUsPerCore() 

// 7 != 6
claimed := (a.numCPUsNeeded == freeCPUs.Size()) 

```

You can see the ablove code block. whether `a.numCPUsNeeded` is 6 or 7, the result of `numCoresNeeded` both equal to 3. When `a.numCPUsNeeded` is 7, claim can never be true.


> Do you have both `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` and `full-pcpus-only` policy options enabled?
> 
> With `full-pcpu-only` policy option we restrict the CPU Manager core allocation algorithm to full physical cores only. In case you have it enabled and are requesting number of CPUs (7 in your case) that is not multiple of cpusPerCore (2) then the failure is expected.

I only enable the `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache`.
/cc @ajcaldelas @wongchar

Yes uncore cache alignment was implemented with the intent that full-pcpus-only would be used to reduce the noisy neighbor issue on SMT-enabled processors. However not a hard requirement for SMT/hyperthreading-disabled processors to enable full-pcpus-only.

I'll look into a fix and bring it up to sig-node.
/triage accepted

title: externalIPs DNAT rules are not installed when clusterIP is None

nodes.body: /sig network

@ttc0419 kube-proxy does noy handle headless services, it ignores headless services, so it is not possible to add ips for those. You can see that iptables kube-proxy behaves the same,


what it seems is a bug in validation for Services, does it make sense for a headless service to have external IPs?
/kind bug


/cc @danwinship @thockin

> [@ttc0419](https://github.com/ttc0419) kube-proxy does noy handle headless services, it ignores headless services, so it is not possible to add ips for those. You can see that iptables kube-proxy behaves the same,
> 
> what it seems is a bug in validation for Services, does it make sense for a headless service to have external IPs? /kind bug
> 
> /cc [@danwinship](https://github.com/danwinship) [@thockin](https://github.com/thockin)

Maybe I want a monolithic service to be only accessible from outside and I do not want to waste a cluster ip for it.

Sure, that's a plausible thing to want, but it's not how Service is designed to work, unfortunately.

Given that `externalIPs` is a kind of deprecated feature due to CVEs anyway, I don't think we want to expand its functionality. It would make more sense to have a `Gateway` pointing to a headless Service. (I'm not sure if that's currently supported, but that seems like the right way to do it.)
for ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/pull/3608

Service API was intended to be "simple"" to use in simple cases. It was not designed to be infinitely flexible.  It sounds like you've hit the end of "simple cases".

Gateway API is intended to be more flexible and composable. That might be a better fit for what you want, but I feel obligated to point out that cluster IPS are virtual and are not usually worth economizing for.

Aside from the feature request for an LB without a clusterIP, this issue exposes a bug.  I am going to repurpose it.

Apparently, validation does not flag an error when:
- `type=ClusterIP`, `clusterIP=None`, and `loadBalancerIP` is set
- `type=ClusterIP`, `clusterIP=None`, and `externalIPs` is set

Note: we DO flag an error when trying to set `loadBalancerSourceRanges`.

Unfortunately, fixing validation bugs is always risky since there's very likely somebody who is using that configuration and it's not failing, even if it doesn't do what they intended.

What we CAN do is add API warnings for these cases.
@thockin  - I see that you've added `help wanted `. Do you plan to submit a PR, or  I can take over this issue?

help-wanted means that we acknowledge the problem and have a pretty good understanding of a fix that a relative newcomer could implement, but the core team is not prioritizing it at the moment.  In other words - go for it!
/assign

It seems like there is a race between `stream` and `readDemuxLoop`.  

Since  `readDemuxLoop` is emitted as a seperated goroutine and the execution order between goroutines does not guarentted, so it is possible that `CreateStream` inside of `stream` has not been called yet, but `getStream` inside of `readDemuxLoop` is called. In this case, a error message like `Unknown stream id 1, discarding message` will be raised.

title: CVE-2025-1974: ingress-nginx admission controller RCE escalation
body:
CVSS Rating: ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)) (Score: 9.8, Critical)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where under certain conditions, an unauthenticated attacker with access to the pod network can achieve arbitrary code execution in the context of the ingress-nginx controller. This can lead to disclosure of Secrets accessible to the controller. (Note that in the default installation, the controller can access all Secrets cluster-wide.)

### Am I vulnerable?

This issue affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running \`kubectl get pods \--all-namespaces \--selector app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx\`.

#### Affected Versions

- < v1.11.0
- v1.11.0 \- 1.11.4  
- v1.12.0

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

**ACTION REQUIRED:** The following steps must be taken to mitigate this vulnerability: Upgrade ingress-nginx to v1.11.5, v1.12.1, or any later version.

Before applying the patch, this issue can be mitigated by disabling the Validating Admission Controller functionality of ingress-nginx.

#### Fixed Versions

- ingress-nginx [main@0ccf4ca](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/pull/13068/commits/0ccf4caaadec919680c455d221e53d97970d527d)

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: [Upgrading Ingress-nginx](https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/deploy/upgrade/)

### Detection

There are no known indicators of compromise that prove this vulnerability has been exploited.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Nir Ohfeld, Ronen Shustin, Sagi Tzadik, and Hillai Ben Sasson from Wiz

The issue was fixed and coordinated by Marco Ebert, James Strong, Tabitha Sable, and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

I'm trying to understand the attack surface for CVE-2025-1974 in our environment where:
- EKS worker nodes are in private subnets
- The ingress-nginx admission controller is only exposed via ClusterIP service
- No public LoadBalancer or NodePort exposure for the admission webhook

My understanding is that this setup provides multiple layers of protection:
1. The admission webhook's ClusterIP is only accessible within the cluster
2. Private subnets prevent direct internet access to the nodes
3. Access would require compromising another workload within the cluster first

However, I'd appreciate clarification on:
- Is this a sufficient security boundary?
- Are there any edge cases where the admission controller could still be exposed?
- Should we still upgrade despite these network controls?

EDIT - Created a new issue to get some traction #131062

Can we please get a k8s network policy that prevents this exploit ASAP? For people who have network policies enabled, it seems like the easiest mitigation mechanism (requiring no changes such as deleting the webhook) would be disabling traffic to it. 

I'm looking into it, but I am unsure what needs access to ingress-nginx-controller-admission.ingress-nginx.svc.cluster.local for example.

EDIT:

I've deleted this network policy because it will not work, still looking to find one that would mitigate this without requiring deletion of anything

EDIT2:

I gave up on a network policy mechanism as it was complex and instead followed the mitigation of deleting the `validating-webhook` lines from the deployment and removing the ingress-nginx-admission ValidatingWebhookConfiguration

@Kingshuk-Kubera I read it as: The admission controller is now less smart. Generated nginx config used to be verified _both_ by the admission controller and by nginx itself at reload. Now, to prevent CVE-2025-1974, only the latter happens.

It means that you are safe, and enabling the admission-controller is safe, but the fix comes with the cost of a slightly higher risk of nginx failing at runtime (at config reload) due to invalid config.

As far as I understand:
This means that any invalid ingress resource could stop any further changes to the Nginx configuration from actually being applied.
This would mean that your ingress would stop "reacting" to any changes in any ingress resource until the resource that is "blocking" the update from working is fixed.
This is basically the same behaviour that existed before the admission webhook was introduced.

vs.

> an unauthenticated attacker with access to the pod network

The pod network isn't routed.
Doesn't that make it AV:A, not AV:N?
**That would lower the score from 9.8 to 8.8 (High).**

For reference, here are the definitions:
<details>
<summary>Attack Vector: Network (AV:N):</summary>
The vulnerable component is bound to the network stack and the set of possible attackers extends beyond the other options listed, up to and including the entire Internet. Such a vulnerability is often termed 'remotely exploitable' and can be thought of as an attack being exploitable at the protocol level one or more network hops away (e.g., across one or more routers).
</details>

<details>
<summary>Attack Vector: Adjacent (AV:A):</summary>
The vulnerable component is bound to the network stack, but the attack is limited at the protocol level to a logically adjacent topology. This can mean an attack must be launched from the same shared physical (e.g., Bluetooth or IEEE 802.11) or logical (e.g., local IP subnet) network, or from within a secure or otherwise limited administrative domain (e.g., MPLS, secure VPN to an administrative network zone).
</details>

It is not directly routable in most of my installations, but in _some_ setups it is. I have customers with DHCP CNI and corp-wide routable service-nets and pod-nets.

Also; in other setups, these nets might not be routable, but the cluster itself is multi-tenancy, so workload in user-namespaces might be less trustworthy. Remember, any pod in _any_ namespace has access to the pod net.

That said; I don't have any opinions on whether the above arguments make it `AV:N` or not.

title: List calls in a k8s 1.34 client will make additional api requests and log a warning w/o watch perms
body:
### What happened?

The WatchList feature is slated to be default-on in k8s 1.34: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/pull/3136#discussion_r1982992848

Due to how it is implemented, this feature requires watch permissions to perform list calls. If that permission doesn't exist, an [api call that is guaranteed to fail](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e319c541f144e9bee6160f1dd8671638a9029f4c/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/gentype/type.go#L178) will be made and [a warning will be logged](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e319c541f144e9bee6160f1dd8671638a9029f4c/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/gentype/type.go#L178).

As a user, it is extremely surprising and unexpected that a LIST call would require watch permissions. In many cases, the users of projects that internally use client-go will be lead into thinking that there is a misconfiguration, which is not the case. 

This feature also completely defeats the purpose of having separate LIST and WATCH permissions in the first place.

### What did you expect to happen?

One or more of:
* This never being on by default in the clients for LIST operations and always requiring explicit opt in
* List calls using WatchList not require watch permissions

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Enable memory limit decrease
body:
/kind bug

When shrinking the pod-level memory limits (sum of container limits iff all containers have limits), the Kubelet checks the current pod memory usage, and doesn't apply the new limits if the new limits < current usage. However, the Kubelet doesn't place the same restriction on containers, and we don't require container runtimes to make the same check.

In practice, this means that for a single container pod, decreasing the memory limit below usage will result in the resize being indefinitely in progress, but for a multiple container pod, if some containers have sufficient free memory, you can shrink the memory limits below usage for a container in the pod, resulting in that container being OOM-killed.

What is the desired behavior here?

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cEFLXKwNOSNLAkzyhoJUgkBW0OiX-9bXB_aJV7OAypw/edit?tab=t.0 provides more background information and several options for how this should be handled.

/sig node
/priority important-soon

nodes.body:
/triage accepted
/milestone v1.33
/assign
/cc

/milestone clear

In v1.33 we are going to forbid decreasing memory limits.

/remove-priority important-soon
/priority backlog

(please fix priority if this adjustment is wrong)

/priority important-longterm

I'd like to at least make progress towards a design for this in the v1.34 timeline. TBD whether this is a GA blocker.
/remove-priority backlog

Wondering if there is a chance to get around the forbidden memory resize in case of restart not required containers.

I have a use case where I have multiple containers in the same pod, a few containers may end with status zero much before another long running container. Today, kubernetes doesn't allow me to mark the resources released as allocatable. I do not expect these containers to come back to life or even if they do due to extreme corner case of garbage collection, they wouldn't be consequential as they will go back to exit code 0 right away due to checkpoints.

With v1.32 and available feature flags, I am able to use resizing very well and release resources not under use easily. However, this issue discussion changes it all.

Forbidding resize in such cases doesn't look useful. I feel users should be allowed to choose the option here.

@santosh-d3vpl3x thank you for sharing your use case. Resizing memory requests should be sufficient to make the resources available to other pods, unless you're dealing with guaranteed pods?

In either case, this is only intended to be a temporary restriction until we figure out what the correct behavior is. The question basically boils down to: if limits are resized below usage and we can't reclaim enough memory, should the resize remain in progress indefinitely, or should we terminate (oomkill) the container?

> The question basically boils down to: if limits are resized below usage and we can't reclaim enough memory, should the resize remain in progress indefinitely, or should we terminate (oomkill) the container?

I believe the choice should be left to the users. Reasoning: given I see both of these to be correct approaches within my own set of use cases, I feel both of these are valid choices and I should be able to configure the behavior I want.

As a flow, it could also be that resize could be given a grace period after which it is OOMKilled. However, I would be cautious of introducing complexity of mixing these two behaviours together before we have a good signal indicating this complexity is totally worth it.

That’s is true , end user is responsible to patch accordingly with the application needs . I assume an operator or another entity with rights to resize will have a way with in-app metrics and check the memory usage before resizing . I understand however also from K8s point of view would be beneficial to have the ability to protect against an OOM situation .

As a consequence of today’s limitation if end user scales up memory please note it cannot scale down memory any longer. I think this contradicts with the previous claimed benefit of InPlacePodVerticalScaling being useful to accelerate startup time from a memory perspective ( ie increasing memory initially and then reducing ) , since we cannot reduce the memory now, for the moment. So yes it will accelerate startup but the memory resources will be under utilized 

In case of kubelet restart during recovery which memory will it maintained ? The original “lower memory” or the new resized “larger memory” ?  If the latest resized memory is maintained then we might end up in a case where kubelet could not start all PoDs ( since for each pod resized memory will be the last max memory )

Above we will need to consider in the journey from Beta to GA , looking forward for more feedback when it is beta. Necessity is the mother of invention :-)

> Resizing memory requests should be sufficient to make the resources available to other pods, unless you're dealing with guaranteed pods?

I have been able to reclaim resources back with no problems at all once the containers were downscaled, works on 1.32.
cc @roycaihw

My concern with providing a guarantee that downsizing memory won't force an oomkill is that if memory spikes right after the limit is decreased, that could still lead to an oomkill, so it seems like the added complexity is not worth it.

If we're not talking about race conditions around memory spikes, then I think this should be addressed by whoever is doing the resizing: look at memory usage (ideally with some history over a time window) before doing the scale-down, and document that scaling down _could_ trigger an oomkill.

I think the oomkill behavior could also be desired: we're talking about decreasing limits, not requests. What if my application has a memory leak, and is causing problems in the system? I want to decrease the limit, even if it triggers an oomkill, to constrain it to the new bounds.

+1 for your concern. 

Also when it comes to consistency, there are features where cgroup versions affect how the same input/condition will make system behave, for example, the oom killer for process groups. 

If cgroups provide no escape hatch, putting a band-aid at the feature level seems like a bad idea.

We should focus on the cgroups v2 behavior since cgroups v1 is in maintenance mode.

In cgroups v2, the behavior of shrinking `memory.max` below the non-reclaimable usage is that it invokes the oomkiller. The workaround is to set `memory.high` as a soft-limit trigger reclaim and throttle new allocations, and then check the usage without risk of a race condition before shrinking `memory.max`. However, this isn't the intended use for memory.high (it's intended to be used with a user-space oomkiller), and there are some warnings about using it along with `memory.max`. More research is necessary.

I'm not convinced this complexity is worth it, especially given the concerns in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129152#issuecomment-2798244734. I'm personally leaning towards just shrinking `memory.max` and letting it invoke the oomkiller as needed, but I'd like to hear more input from the community.
/assign @roycaihw

/milestone v1.34
/assign @tallclair 

I'd like to re-enable memory limit decrease in v1.34. From offline discussions, I think the right behavior is to best-effort avoid triggering an oomkill:

- In nodes up to v1.33, the kubelet checks the pod's memory usage before lowering the limit, but doesn't perform a container-level check
- In v1.34, we should reenable memory limit decrease in the API (validation), and add in a container-level check (@tallclair)
- We can look for further improvements by leveraging kernel mechanisms in subsequent releases (@roycaihw)

Hello @tallclair 
This issue has not been updated for 6 weeks, so I'd like to check the status. If there's anything we can do, please let us know.
The code freeze is starting 02:00 UTC Friday 25th July 2025 (about 3 weeks from now). Please make sure the PR has both lgtm and approved labels before the code freeze. Thanks!
The KEP update for this was approved last week, so we should be good-to-go on this one. Plan is to relax the restriction in v1.34.

body:
### What happened?

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - image: alpine
    command:
      - sleep
      - "10000"
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    name: alpine
  dnsPolicy: None
  dnsConfig:
    nameservers:
    - "192.168.0.10"
    searches:
    - .
    - default.svc.cluster.local
    - svc.cluster.local
    - cluster.local
    options:

      value: "3"
```

Applying this pod YAML to Kubernetes will result in an error like this:


hi @zengyuxing007  
I encountered the error when setting dnsConfig.searches to a dot (".") in a Pod spec. Here’s the error:

```The Pod "test" is invalid: spec.dnsConfig.searches[0]: Invalid value: "": a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters, '-' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'example.com', regex used for validation is '[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*')```

This seems inconsistent with Unix /etc/resolv.conf standards.

In Unix-like systems, setting a single dot as a search path in `resolv.conf` is used to prevent DNS suffixes from being appended to a domain query. 

This functionality is crucial for specific network configurations and might be beneficial for Kubernetes users to have.
Could we look into aligning Kubernetes' DNS config validations with these Unix standards?

Given the potential for enhancing DNS configuration flexibility in Kubernetes, I believe revising this validation could be valuable. 

Would it be possible to discuss this in an upcoming SIG-Network meeting, or should we consider starting a thread to gather more community feedback?

title: StatefulSet with podManagementPolicy=OrderedReady and minReadySeconds does not scale down correctly
body:
### What happened?

1. create the OrderedReady statefulset

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-roll
spec:
  replicas: 2
  minReadySeconds: 30
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx-roll
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx-roll
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: ghcr.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: web
```


2. wait for the 2nd pod to become ready, but not available (can also happen when the pod has lost availability)
3. scale the statefulset to 1 replica
 
```
kubectl scale statefulset nginx-roll --replicas=1
```

4. the 2nd pod should start terminating immediately but instead it hangs until the KCM is fully resynced


### What did you expect to happen?

the 2nd pod should start terminating immediately

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

see `What happened?` 

### Anything else we need to know?

we can see in the logs that the syncs are happening but the firstUnhealthyPod variable is not resolved, so the progress is stalled

```
stateful_set_control.go:509] "StatefulSet is waiting for Pod to be Available prior to scale down" statefulSet="test/nginx-roll" pod=""
```

We even get  the availability check scheduled and called, but because a prior scheduling already ocurred, the new check is thrown away (should not happen, but a similar issue was reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119352 and a fix is blocked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112328)

```
stateful_set.go:243] "StatefulSet will be enqueued after minReadySeconds for availability check" statefulSet="test/nginx-roll" minReadySeconds=30
```

the sync will be called too soon and resolves again in 
```
stateful_set_control.go:509] "StatefulSet is waiting for Pod to be Available prior to scale down" statefulSet="test/nginx-roll" pod=""
```

The next sync will ocurr when KCM is fully resynced which can be a long time (depending on KCM resync period)



statefulset controller should scale down the first condemned pod as soon as it can, but keep the predecessor pods running available

```console
$ kubectl version

Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
```
